questions.stem: In sea water, which term names the salt?

options.explanation: The salt is the substance that dissolves, which is exactly the solute's role.
The solvent is the liquid doing the dissolving; in sea water that is the water, not the salt.
options.misconception: swaps the roles of solute and solvent

options.explanation: The solution is the whole mixture of salt and water together, not the salt on its own.
options.misconception: names the mixture rather than the dissolved substance

options.explanation: Saturation describes a solution holding the maximum dissolved solute; it is not a name for the salt itself.
options.misconception: attaches saturation to any dissolved substance

questions.stem: A solution holding the greatest amount of dissolved solute it can is called...

options.explanation: Saturation means no more solute can dissolve; the solution is full to its limit.
Insoluble means a substance will not dissolve at all; saturation is about having dissolved the maximum already.
The solvent is only the liquid; saturation describes the state of the whole solution.
options.misconception: applies a component term to the whole mixture

options.explanation: Dilute describes a solution with little solute, the opposite of saturated.

questions.stem: Sand sits in a beaker of water without dissolving. Which term describes the sand?

options.explanation: A substance that will not dissolve is insoluble, exactly as the note's example records for sand.
Soluble means able to dissolve; the sand demonstrably has not.
options.misconception: reverses the term for a non-dissolving substance

options.explanation: The solvent is the liquid; the sand is the solid sitting in it.
options.misconception: uses the liquid's term for the solid

options.explanation: Saturation describes how much has dissolved in the solution, not a substance that refuses to dissolve.
options.misconception: applies a mixture-level term to a single substance

questions.stem: Which pairing of term and sea-water example is correct?

options.text: Solvent — the water in sea water
options.explanation: The water is the liquid doing the dissolving, which is the solvent's definition.

options.text: Solute — the water in sea water
options.explanation: The water does the dissolving; the salt, not the water, is the solute.
options.misconception: assigns the solvent's example to the solute

options.text: Solution — the salt on its own
options.explanation: The solution is the whole mixture, salt and water together.
options.misconception: names only part of the mixture as the solution

options.explanation: The note's saturation example is sea water in the Dead Sea, water already holding its maximum salt.
options.misconception: treats any natural water as saturated

questions.stem: Which statement about the four terms is true?
questions.misconceptionClass: relational understanding of the term set

options.text: The solute dissolves in the solvent to form the solution
options.explanation: This is the relationship the definitions build: solute plus solvent gives the solution.

options.text: The solvent dissolves in the solute to form the solution
options.explanation: The roles are reversed: the liquid is never the substance that disappears.
options.misconception: reverses solute and solvent in the relationship

options.text: A saturated solution can still dissolve more solute at the same temperature
options.explanation: Saturated means the maximum is already dissolved; nothing more fits at that temperature.
options.misconception: misses the maximum limit in the saturation definition

options.text: Soluble substances never take part in solutions
options.explanation: Soluble substances are precisely the ones that dissolve to form solutions.

questions.stem: A cup of sugar water is made by stirring sugar into hot tea. State which substance is the solvent.
questions.modelAnswer: The tea (the water in it) is the solvent — the liquid doing the dissolving.

questions.stem: State the term for the mixture formed once a solute has dissolved in a solvent.
Explain why no more salt can dissolve in a solution that is already saturated.
questions.modelAnswer: Because a saturated solution already holds the maximum amount of dissolved solute the solvent can take, so no more solute can be dissolved.

questions.stem: A student keeps stirring sugar into tea until some sugar sits at the bottom and will not dissolve, however long they stir. State the term describing the tea at that moment.
questions.modelAnswer: The tea is a saturated solution — it holds the maximum amount of dissolved solute the solvent can take.
